Desperate Affray on the Peninsula.

FORT MONROE, VA., December 28.—A disturbance occurred on Friday evening at Smithville, fifteen miles west of here, between a white man named Dunn and a party of colored men, who had met to organize a military company. One of the men caught Dunn by his whiskers and slapped his face, whereupon he drew a single-barrelled pistol and killed the negro. Dunn than ran into a store and loaded his pistol, and when the crowd, headed by Dan. Cook, with drawn sword, attacked him, he shot Cook dead in his tracks; after which he drew a butcher knife and cut his way out. One man, named Ed. Drew, was badly cut in the abdomen, and will probably die, while others were more or less injured. Dunn gave himself up, and is now in jail at Williamsburg. Intense excitement prevails among the colored people on the Peninsula.

TWO NEGROES SHOT BY A WHITE MAN.
FORTRESS MONROE, Dec. 28.—A disturbance occurred Friday evening at Smithville, fifteen miles west of here, between a white man named Dunn and several colored men who had met to organize a military company. One of the negroes slapped Dunn's face, whereupon the latter drew a pistol and killed his assailant. Dunn then ran into a store and loaded his pistol. A crowd, headed by Daniel Cook, who carried a drawn sword, broke into the store and attacked him. He shot Cook dead, after which he seized a butcher's knife and cut his way out. One man named Edward Drew was badly cut in the abdomen and will probably die; others were more or less injured. Dunn gave himself up and is now in jail at Williamaburg. Intense excitement prevails among the colored people of the peninsula.

PHOTOGRAPHY. The Tribune. WEDNESDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1880.
A meeting called for the purpose of reorganizing the New York Democracy was held at Cooper Institute last night, under the Presidency of Franklin Edson. Abram S. Hewitt, Oswald Ottendorfer, Henry L. Hognet, Allan Campbell, Pierre Lorillard, and other prominent Democrats were present. A declaration of principles, embracing free trade, free ships, hard money, opposition to the use of troops at the polls, and to the assessing of officeholders for political purposes, was adopted. Mr. Hewitt reviewed the cause of the Democratic defeat in the late November election. He attributed it to the compromise of principle on the part of the Democratic leaders. He condemned the coquetting with the Greenbackers in Maine and Indiana and with the Protectionists in New Jersey and Connecticut. He attributed the falling off of the Democratic majority in New York City to the Boss system. He said that Tammany Hall was a thing of the past, and that Irving Hall had also outlived its usefulness. A committee to reorganize the New York Democracy was then appointed.

The trial of Parnell and his fellow-traversers was commenced yesterday in the Court of Queen's Bench before Judges Fitzgerald and Barry. Judgo May, whose recent stump speech from the Bench has been severely commented on by the English press, stated that on account of the criticism on his attitude he felt it his duty to retire from the trial of the case. It is believed that he did so at the request of Secretary Forster. Judge O'Brien, the other member of the Court of Queen's Bench, was unable to be present through ill-health. Only eighteen of the twenty-four jurors answered to their names. The Crown wanted a postponement, but the counsel for the traversers successfully resisted this proposition, which indicates that they were satisfied with the complexion of the panel. The jury selected consists of eight Catholics, three Protestants, and one Quaker. The counsel for Parnell and his companions count on an acquittal, and there is scarcely a chance of conviction.

At a meeting of the Ohio State Bar Association, held at Columbus yesterday, and which was attended by about 300 lawyers, an elaborate plan for the reconstruction and reform of the State Judiciary was submitted. The plan provides that the judicial system of Ohio shall consist of Justice Courts, Probate Courts, a Court of Common Pleas, and a Supreme Court to consist of nine members, to be elected by the people, three at a time, on the minority plan. The jurisdiction of each Court is clearly defined, and a plan for disposing of accumulated business before the Supreme Court is provided for by the proposition to divide the Supreme Court into two branches, the decision of each branch being final when the Judges are unanimous, but when there is a disagreement the whole Court will have to agree on the case. The delegates attending the meeting were banqueted in the evening by the members of the Franklin County Bar.

ON Friday a number of colored men assembled at Smithville, N. C., to organize a colored company. One white man named Dunn attended. A dispute arose, and one of the colored men slapped Dunn in the face. Dunn fatally shot his assailant, and then took refuge in a grocery store, where he re-loaded his pistol. The negroes, headed by one Dan Cook, attacked the house. Dunn shot Cook, and then, arming himself with a butcher's knife, cut his way through the crowd, killing one of them and wounding others. He has surrendered himself to the authorities at Williamsburg. The colored men threaten to take him from the jail and lynch him.

"BILLY THE KID'S" gang of outlaws, cutthroats, and murderers, which has for some time been the terror of Eastern New Mexico, was broken up last Saturday morning by Deputy-Sheriff Garrett, of Santa Fé, and his posse. Two of the outlaws were killed and four of them were captured and lodged in the Las Vegas Jail. Monday afternoon the prisoners were taken to Santa Fé, notwithstanding the threatened resistance of Sheriff Powers and the citizens of Las Vegas, who were rather anxious to get possession of the prisoners that they might lynch them.

A TRIBUNE representative yesterday interviewed several of the leading members of the Board of Trade on the question of the proposed change of quarters to the Scott property on the corner of La Salle and Jackson streets, and found them all but unanimously in favor of the change and the acceptance of the Scott proposition. The Committee of the Chamber of Commerce has offered to enlarge and improve the present quarters, but it is not believed that the contemplated improvement and enlargement could meet the circumstances of the case.

At the meeting of the Home-Rule members in Dublin, Monday, it was resolved to oppose the suspension of the Habeas Corpus act, or any other coercive measure for Ireland, to the last extremity. The members pledged themselves to act as one man in opposition to any such measures. Mr. Forster has promised to bring in a bill soon for the assimilation of the Irish municipal franchise to that of England. He also indicated that a measure for the extension of the franchise in counties throughout Great Britain and Ireland was part of the Liberal program.

Mr. A. T. Mousk, the resident buyer of Harwood, the Minneapolis clothier, has made some very interesting disclosures about the very extensive purchases made by his employer a few months before the failure. Harwood seemed very desirous of getting as large a stock on credit as possible, and without regard to the necessities of his trade. It is stated on other authority that Ingram, the New York buyer in whose favor Harwood confessed judgment for $830,620, owed the firm over $500. Harwood has not been heard of since Friday.

A fire broke out in Reed & Burton's confectionery establishment at Quincy early yesterday morning, and extended to the adjoining houses. The store in which the fire originated and the stock were damaged $7,500 worth. Joseph & Nilke's stock of dry goods, worth $15,000, was destroyed, and L. Ward's loss on building is $9,500. Huffman & Kingsbaker Bros., tobaccoists, suffer slight loss.

Tinnules, the intermeddler who has caused so much noise about Secretary Schurz's treatment of the Poncas, was examined yesterday by Senators Kirkwood and Dawes, of

the Senate Investigating Committee. He admitted that he went to the Ponca settlement in Indian Territory to persuade the Indians to return to Dakota, so as to make a case for the United States Supreme Court, and otherwise acted as an intermeddler and a busybody. He excused himself by saying that he only acted as agent for certain parties in Omaha.

The official statement of the population of twenty-two States and six Territories is made public this morning. From this statement it appears that the population of Iowa is 1,024,403; Kentucky, 1,048,500; Wisconsin, 1,315,380; Kansas, 935,335. The population of Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio is not yet given. New York State has a population of 5,082,844, while Nevada has only 62,205. Massachusetts has 1,783,080, and Delaware only 140,654 people. Utah has 143,907, and Wyoming only 20,788. The population of the District of Columbia is 177,638.

THE TRIBUNE presents to its readers this morning Mrs. Zelda Seguin's (Mrs. Wallace's) version of the reasons which led to her withdrawal from the Abbott Opera Company, the injustice which she suffered at the hands of Mr. Wetherell, the manager of the company, and the efforts of Mr. Morrissey, the press agent, to lower her in the estimation of the public. The brilliant contralto tells her story in a piquant way, and whatever she forgot about the trouble was supplied to THE TRIBUNE representative by her spouse, Mr. Wallace.

ATTACKED BY A CROWD OF NEGROES. Killing Two and Cutting his Way Through the Others With a Sheath Knife.
FORTRESS MONROE, Dec. 28.—On the evening of the 24th inst., a row occurred at Smithville, a small collection of houses on the road from Hampton to Yorktown, and more generally known as the "Half-way House," in which two colored men were shot and instantly killed, and two more badly cut, by Howard Dunn, a white farmer of that vicinity. From a number of reports, which are somewhat conflicting, the following particulars are gathered:

It seems that Dunn, who owns a large farm, has had notices posted warning the public not to hunt on his premises, and it was also reported that he had threatened to shoot any one he found trespassing. On the afternoon of the 24th a large crowd of colored people congregated at the Half-way House to organize a militia company, and probably to begin the Christmas festivities. They had been drinking somewhat freely, and when Dunn came up they began to chaff him about shooting any one he found gunning on his farm, one or two declaring that they were going to go out that afternoon and shoot over his place. Dunn is said to have taken their badinage in good temper, wishing, if possible, to avoid a quarrel; but it seemed to be the purpose of the negroes to provoke a fight, for one of them went up to Dunn, caught him by the chin whiskers, pulled them vigorously, and slapped him in the face. Dunn is a small man, weighing not over 100 pounds. He quickly released himself, and, drawing a small single-barrelled pistol, shot his assailant dead at his feet. He then retreated into the store, concealed himself behind the counter, and reloaded his pistol, at the same time arming himself with a sheath knife for future emergencies.

By this time the store was thronged, and a negro named Dan Cook, who was armed with a sword, as the prospective Captain of the company, demanded where that — was who had shot his friend. At this Dunn showed himself and said he was the man. Cook then attempted to draw his sword, but while in the act Dunn took aim and shot him through the neck, killing him almost instantly. Dunn then backed into a corner and drew his knife, while the crowd closed in on him. The first one (Ed Drew) who came within his reach, received a frightful and, perhaps, fatal wound in the abdomen, another was cut in the hand, and Dunn, advancing, literally cut his way out of the crowd, which seemed paralyzed at his coolness, and made his escape. He ran to the nearest magistrate and gave himself up, but the Judge, fearing a reaction, and that a mob might be collected to lynch him, sent him in charge of a deputy sheriff to the jail in Williamsburg, where he is now confined.

Dunn is about 40 years old, and served during the war in a Virginia regiment from the lower peninsula, of which Judge Willis of Hampton was Colonel. The Judge speaks of him as an excellent soldier, who was noted for his bravery and coolness in action. The affair has created intense excitement in this section. Dunn's friends claiming that he acted entirely in self-defence. The Grand Jury meets in about ten days, when the case will come up for trial.

Last Friday morning was so cold that few persons got up in time to see the solar eclipse, but all have had a fine opportunity to witness the eclipse of the earth from that time until the present.—It has been many years since Bristol has had so deep and so permanent a snow.

The Abingdon Virginian says Mr. Thomas Cowan of Lebanon died suddenly, after eating a hearty dinner on Tuesday before Christmas.

The office of the Burkeville Sentinel was completely destroyed by fire Dec. 22. Mr. Alphens Bolling, the proprietor had no insurance.

The Midland R. R. has been sold to a syndicate in the interest of the B. & O. for six and a half millions, and the sale has been confirmed by Judge Keith.

Dr. E. H. Chapin, the celebrated Universalist preacher of N. Y. died during the holidays. He commenced his career at a now defunct Universalist church in Richmond, Va. At last he has obeyed that law which we all agree to be universal, and has passed in his chips.

The real and personal assessment of Tennessee is only $211,000,000. Though exceeding Va. in population, she falls behind the old Dominion some 100 millions in her taxable basis. She has lost about that amount since 1873.

Judge Hughes says in effect "no, gentlemen, you have shown yourselves rather poor hands at running the Piedmont & Arlington Life Insurance Co., to handle its property any longer. I appoint Mr. Boulevard Receiver, and you will please pass over the books and box to him.

Judge Hunter Marshall recently fell on the frozen pavement in Richmond and broke his leg, and Lieut. Schwatka, after climbing all the ice in the polar region, and burying the bones of Sir John Franklin's men, fell in New York and broke one of his legs also.

Old Chief, the vicious elephant of Jno Robinson's circus is still using up his keepers. Not satisfied with killing Jno. King at Charlotte, N. C., he wrapped his trunk about Tom Sullivan's body, squeezing him to his satisfaction, dropped him to the ground about as limp as a wet sponge. Sullivan was Old John's Master of transportation, and was drunk. Old Chief was sober, and his victim had to be taken to the hospital.

We cannot epitomize a tenth of the R. R. accidents, shootings, burnings, stab-bings, murders and lynchings that have rendered this holiday season famous, but a case that occurred at Smithfield, near Hampton Va., the day before Christmas, is rather too rare a one to overlook. Howard Dunn shot and killed a negro, who attacked him. The other negroes then in a great crowd waited on him and dared him to come out. He did so, shot the ring leader and stabbed another one, killing both. Three negro corpses in one day as the work of one man, would seem to imply a fair amount of whiskey.

The President of the Swiss Republic Committed Suicide during Christmas. The small majority by which he was elected is one of the depressing causes. In America we sometimes have Presidents who were elected by no majority at all, except that on certain Returning Boards, and they don't suicide at all—though they ought to.

In population Tennessee is a little ahead of Virginia, the former having 1,542,463, and the latter 1,512,220—difference 40,243. West Va. has 618,193, and if Va. had what has been stolen from her she would number smartly more than two millions. The great empire State of Georgia lacks 4585 of having as many people as Tenn.

Mr. Jacob Hamilton of New Canton, Hawkins county, Tenn, father-in-law of Dr. G. Cate, at Blountville, died Saturday, Dec. 18th, aged 52 years. He had been in bad health for a year. The Rogersville Spectator properly says he was widely known and esteemed, and was one of the best and most energetic citizens of Hawkins county.

Columbus Gregory was run over and killed by the western bound mail train at Abingdon, Saturday the 18th of Dec. His head was severed from the body, which was horribly mutilated. When last seen he was intoxicated.

BRIEFs.—The March term of our county court, held on Monday, brought to our town a number of the residents of the county

Mrs. M. B Funsten, widow of the late Col. O. R. Funsten of this county, died in Alexandria on the 2nd inst. She was a daughter of the late James Bowen of Albemarle county.

An engine and baggage-car of the S. V. R. R. were partly thrown from the track, in shifting at the Charlestown depot, on Tuesday evening of last week, causing a detention of four or five trains for a short while, but doing no serious damage.

Winchester Presbytery will hold its next meeting at Elk Branch Church, in Jeffer-county, beginning April 13th, at 3 o'clock P. M.

The telegraph line on the S. V. R. R. is now completed, and in working trim, all the way through from Hagerstown to Waynesboro.

Rev. F. A. Strother left Berryville the first of last week to attend the annual Conference of the M. E. Church South, held in Harrisonburg.

Last Thursday felt more Spring-like than any day since the beginning of the present year. Friday, however, the air was cold; Saturday evening some rain and sleet fell; Sunday and Monday cloudy weather, with brisk winds prevailing the last named day.

The board of supervisors of this county met on Saturday last and closed the levy account. It was decided to retain the same rate of taxation imposed last year for county and railroad purposes—to-wit, 10 cents on the $100 for county purposes and 30 cents on the $100 to meet the interest and provide a sinking fund for the bonds issued to the S. V. R. R. Co.

We are glad that our board of supervisors ordered new registration books and caused the several registrars of the county to copy the registration lists into the new books. The old books had become very much mutilated.

The Black-birds have arrived in large flocks, and they make the woods echo with their matin songs. Out of consideration for the birds, if not for man, we hope Vennor will leave off giving us bad weather.

To-day, Thursday, the 17th, is St. Patrick's day, when, according to Vennor, we are to be visited again with snow storms, high winds, &c.

The snow has generally disappeared from the valley, but the Blue Ridge mountains continue to present to us a white face, owing to the presence of snow.

The Shenandoah river was full all of last week, but it did not get beyond its banks.

Straw is becoming scarce in the county, but fodder is plentiful because the hard winter caught most of it out in the fields.

By referring to our new advertisements it will be seen that Dr. Fuller, dentist, of Winchester, has resumed the practice of his profession, which was interrupted by an accident that recently befell him in that city.

Parties wishing to purchase some ewes with their lambs are directed to the advertisement of Dr. C. E. Lippitt, which appears in another column.

Mr. D. H. Sowers is prepared to take orders for trees and furnish strawberry plants to all who are in want of them. He represents the nurseries of A. B. Davis, of Loudoun county.

It is learned from reliable source that the Shenandoah Valley Railroad Company has finally decided upon Big Lick, Roanoke county, Va., as the objective point, and possibly the terminus, of the proposed extension of that road. A meeting of the stockholders has been called for the 5th of April at Luray, Va.

The dogs last week attacked Mr. R. Powell Page's flock of sheep and killed one ewe and two lambs.

In a conversation with some of our farmers this week they expressed fears that the wheat crop has been severely injured by the recent wet and freezing weather.

The first issue contains a statement as to how these troops happened to be quartered in Berryville. The Enlarged Illinois Canal.
To the Editor of The Chicago Tribune.

FAMILY, Ill., April 9.—Do the real friends of this work realize that the first practical step forward is now about to be frustrated, and that if so, two years more delay will be inevitable? The dead apathy and neglect that appears to prevail, would seem to indicate that they do not realize the dangerous situation of affairs. If the bill long since introduced before the Illinois Legislature by Senator Whiting can pass before adjournment, then in November the people of Illinois can vote the conditional transfer to the United States, and then, and not till then, the matter can be brought properly before Congress and the country for decisive and practical action; and thus the intolerable delay, error, and secret and indirect opposition from various sources, at home and abroad, through various pretences and various forms of error, can probably soon be made to give way to common interests, actual work, and accomplished results. But if this necessary legal step is now defeated by delay or other means, then all must wait for the next session of the Illinois Legislature two years hence. This would be highly injurious and unnecessary. And all that the enemy need to kill the bill, and so put the matter off for two years longer at least, is just a little more delay, that may be caused by pretended friends. And the delay is very liable to occur, as usual, unless there is some native movement or agitation of the matter.

Fifty-eight years have elapsed since legislation began looking to this moderate work—an adequate and suitable connection between the Great Lake and Mississippi systems, via the Illinois River and Canal. And now every right and just interest in all this land looking to the welfare, safety, and happiness of its people demand that it should be completed at once.

The benefits will soon then be felt in twenty-three great States situated upon those interior waters,—than for the first enjoying this improved island navigation.

And all the great public economies of the entire country conductive to sound, general, and real prosperity among all its people will be promoted by the full use of those great natural organs as prepared for our use by the Creative Wisdom through cons of ages.
noted by the full use of those great natural organs as prepared for our use by the Creative Wisdom through cons of ages.

And there are very peculiar and urgent reasons why further delay would be criminal and dangerous, and should not be endured or tolerated. But apathy and indifference will not ward off this danger or trenchery to interests that none should neglect or disregard if they would do their duty as citizens and as men.

No prefacts whatever should be allowed to cause the people of Illinois to lose the opportunity of voting on this question in November next in accordance with this bill, with the recommendation of the Governor, with the Constitution of the State, and with great and urgent necessities, and with the common safety, interests, and welfare of all.

W. T. S.

Lovely State of Affairs at Yorktown, Va.
To the Editor of The Chicago Tribune.

Yorktown, Va., April 6.—I will now attempt to detail to you some of the doings of our quiet village. On last Christmas Eve a drunken white man shot and killed two innocent colored men in a store a few miles below here, and stabbed another so badly that he is now confined to his bed. The culprit was arraigned last courtday in this town for trial, and a more tareical trial could not be produced by any set of thoutrical performers in the world. The regular County Judge could not face the public after sitting on a case which he knew could not in any legal sense be excused, and therefore he excused himself under the protest of going to the inauguration,—where he did not go,—by sending a judge from the upper part of this district, who had been a Colonel in the Rebel army, to try this case. I was an eye-witness to this whole trial, and I do say without fear of contradiction by any truthful person that there was not even the slightest cause or provocation for striking the victims, much less than shooting two outright, as was unequivocally proven, and finally wounding the third, all of whom were men of large families; and this by a notorious drunken not who is always in some difficulty. The plea set up before the jury by his counsel was, that these men were negroes, and the prisoner a bold ex-Confederate soldier, who had waded his show-soles deep in the blood of negroes and Yankees during the War. The jury, all of whom were ex-Confederates, were morally compelled, after the appeals made to them of the horrible deeds of this double murderer, to acquit him.

It is useless, after this sham trial of a rebel foul in human form, almost at the threshold of the Nation's Capitol, to hereafter try to deny the wholesale murdering of negroes further south. The colored people resolved to hold on the 29 of March an indignation meeting to show to the world that they, after this outrage, weakly submitted to this force, entitled the trial of William H. Dunn, and permitted him to return to his family unguarded and unmolested by any one, and that, too, when they number two to one in this county. To show also that they are unprotected by the laws of the land, when for smaller offenses they are lynched to the first tree without so much as a hearing, however humbly they demean themselves, or submissive and law-abiding. The doubles of the Southern Democratic Rebels that negroes are shunned because they are by the laws of nature negroes and in sympathy with the Republicans is false to the core. So much afraid were those Rebels that this human outrage would be brought to public notice by the meeting before mentioned (March 29) that one of them, having a spark of shame left, important and made overtures to the gettors-up of said meeting several days prior to give it up. Not succeeding in his persuasions, he then threatened all prominent parties to it with being tried for contempt of court, etc. The meeting, however, wont on, and a Committee was appointed to draft resolutions.

The truthfulness of the above statements I will swear to, and knowing your character for fair dealing between man and man, irrespective of his color, and also the just and fearless position of the Tribune, I hope this letter will appear in its columns.

The C. & O. Railroad is at work building a road from Richmond to Newport News, and promises to have a branch running to this place by July 1, or at least in time for the Yorktown Continental, which is going to be a grand affair. The Centennial Association has purchased the temple farm (Halstond's), 600 acres, and intend to lay it out into a grand park, to be called Lafayette Park, and present it to the

United States Government. They also propose to build several wharves in front of Yorktown, and open up all the streets leading to the river. We expect to be daily visited by from 2,000 to 3,000 people during the Centennial. Each State of the original thirteen will have a house in the park, also the United States Government and the French; in fact, the Centennial is booming. ROBERT G. GUFFIN.

CORRECTION O. Nov. 48. Steamer Packers
Two Negroes Killed and Two Seriously Wounded.
CINCINNATI, O., Nov. 29.—Steamer Buckeye State reports a serious riot on the steamer Dacotah near Cattleburg, where she landed. The crew consisted of twenty-two negroes and four white men, and there had been considerable trouble. After the crew were paid off but before leaving the negroes made an attack on the mate, when the second mate and the four white men went to his assistance and a bloody fight ensued, in which two negroes were shot and seriously wounded and two others killed with a monkey wrench and axe, and the remaining negroes driven from the boat.

The boat was on her way to Huntington deeply laden, and was compelled to go to the bank five miles below Catlettsburg, Ky., on account of low water. The boat's deck crew consisted of twenty-two negroes and four white men, exclusive of the officers. There had been some trouble between the mate and the negroes. After laying up, the crew was paid off and the negroes furnished with transportation tickets to Cairo. Before leaving, however, they made an attack on the mate, when the second mate and four white men went to his assistance. A bloody fight ensued, in which two negroes were shot and seriously wounded, and two negroes killed with a monkey-wrench and ax, after which the remaining negroes were driven from the boat. We were unable to learn any names, except that of John Craft, the second mate, who, it is reported, did the shooting.

Diamond Cut Diamond.
Special Dispatch to The Bee.

New York, November 29—4 p. m. The solution of the recent sudden rise in Lake Erie & Western stock is solved by the announcement that a syndicate of capitalists has been formed, who have subscribed sufficient funds for the immediate construction of an important extension to the road, which will probably make the line an assured success. Large stock purchases have been made, principally by the different members of the syndicate. It is stated that the bears on the stock market headed by Gould and Sage, have locked up about $12,000,000, and they will make a fierce struggle this week to break down the stock market through a twist in the money market. These parties last Friday locked up $300,000 in certified checks. The bull combination is stronger than ever, and it is said that $50,000,000 have been borrowed in London on Vanderbilt stocks alone. Mr. Vanderbilt on Saturday ordered the manufacture of fifty locomotive engines for the use of his system of railroads, and the contract has been signed.

Foundry Burned.

Special Dispatch to the Bee.

MATTOON, Ill., November 29—4 p. m. The extensive works of the Mattoon foundry, owned by William Lennox & Co., were entirely destroyed by fire Saturday night. Loss, $20,000. Insurance, $6500. This was the only foundry west of Pittsburg which made the Baldwin cylinder. All the castings used by the machine shops of the Indianapolis and St. Louis railroad were made here.

The S eakershi.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

WASPINGTON, November 29 — 4 p. m.—The Post Sunday morning printed the following: The gossip about the speakership of the next house grows in interest and in importance as members of congress arrive. The general drift of talk brings down the contest to two candidates, and the long list of possible candidates first mentioned are being dropped one after the other for reasons which appears patent to everybody but the candidates themselves and their friends. For instance, Mr. Frye, of Malne, who loomed up as a formidable competitor for the place, is said to be desirous of stepping into the Hon. Hannibal Hamlin's shoes, and that fact precludes the possibility of his occupying the speaker's chair. The same charge is laid at the door of Mr. Conger, of Michigan. The contest between the Bayley and Baldwin factions is very bitter, and their strength is evenly balanced. Herein lies Conger's only hope that of becoming a compromise candidate. There remains, according to this way of looking at the matter, but two prominent candidates. Mr. Burrows, of Michigan, and Mr. Kasson, of Iowa. The former gentleman is already on the ground, and the latter has returned to his diplomatic position in Austria, but his friends are sharply watching the drift of things.

Peached on by a Pard.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

KANSAS CITY, November 29 — 4 p. m.—Two men, Talby and Rose, were arrested at Independence, Missouri, twelve miles from this city, last night, charged with complicity in the Glendale train robbery which occurred in October 1879 by which the Chicago and Alton railway company was a heavy loser. They were spotted through a confession made by a man named Baasham, who has been in jail here, awaiting trial, for several months and who pleaded guilty. Baasham gave a full account of the robbery and the names of the six men connected with it, and it is thought all will be apprehended.

Edison's Electric Light.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

New York, November 29, 4 p. m. — Edison has proposed to make a public test of his system of electric light in a fortnight, and to begin operations in New York in January or February. A number of New York and several Swiss engineers have been invited to witness the test. Edison says he has got his lamps now so that they will burn about six hundred hours, and when a lamp has been used, say five hours a day, not over three lamps a year will be used.

Old and Full of Years.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

Bronson, O., November 29, 4 p. m. — The funeral yesterday of the colored woman, Agnes Brown, was the most remarkable occurrence that ever took place in this county. The deceased died at the age of 120 years and the funeral sermon was preached by an old time acquaintance from Xenia, Ohio, who is in his one hundredth year and has been in the ministry since 1802.

Exiled Socialists.

Special dispatch to The Bee.

New York, November 29—4 p. m. — The committee of New York socialists to receive their expatriated brethren now on their way to this country, has been sitting five days waiting for the arrival of the steamer "Secilia."

The socialists of New York and other cities have made all possible preparations to provide the exiles with work on their arrival here. The majority of these are cigar makers and printers. There are also several newspaper writers.

A Mail Car Burns.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

MARSHALL, Tex., November 29—4 p.m.—The burning of a mail car on the Iron Mountain railroad last Thursday destroyed all the mail matter for Texas and Western Louisiana, except a single pouch, and all the passengers' baggage but two trunks. One of the lost trunks is said to have contained a large amount of money, nearly all greenbacks.

A Bloody Fight.

Special Dispatch to The Bee

CLEVELAND, O., November 29, 4 p.m.—The steamer "Buckeye State" reports a serious riot on the steamer "Dacotah" near Cutlessburg where she landed on account of low water. The crew consisted of twenty-two negroes and four white men and there had been considerable trouble on the trip. After laying up, the crew were paid off and the negroes furnished with transportation tickets to Cairo. Before leaving however, they made an attack on the mate, when the second mate and four white men went to his assistance. A bloody fight ensued, in which two negroes were shot and seriously wounded, and two negroes killed with a monkey wrench, after which the remaining negroes were driven from the boat.
